steps.title: A tree in an array
steps.caption: Each parent ≤ its children, so the minimum is on top; filled level by level, it fits an array.
steps.body: A **min-heap** keeps two rules. *Order*: every parent is at most its children, so the smallest item is always the root and `peek` is O(1). *Shape*: the tree is complete, filled level by level from the left, so it packs into an array with no pointers: the children of index `i` sit at `2i + 1` and `2i + 2` and its parent at `(i − 1) // 2` (4, at index 1, has its parent at 0 and its children at 3 and 4).

steps.title: Push: sift up
steps.caption: push(3): append at index 7, swap up while smaller than the parent: past 7 and 4, stop under 1.
steps.body: `push(3)` appends 3 at the next free slot, index 7, which keeps the shape. It then **sifts up**: while 3 is smaller than its parent at `(i − 1) // 2` the two swap, so it passes 7, then 4, and stops under 1: 3 comparisons, 2 swaps. A complete tree of n items has ⌊log₂ n⌋ + 1 levels and each swap climbs one, so push is O(log n).

steps.title: Pop: sift down
steps.caption: pop() returns 1; the last item, 7, takes the root and sinks past the smaller child: 2, then 6.
steps.body: `pop()` returns the root, 1. To keep the tree complete, the last item, 7, moves to the root and **sifts down**: it swaps with the smaller child while that child is smaller than it (2, then 6) and stops at index 5, which has no children: 4 comparisons, 2 swaps. Again at most one swap per level, so pop is O(log n).

steps.title: Heapsort and uses
steps.caption: Popping until empty yields 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 9: heapsort, O(n log n) even in the worst case.
steps.body: Popping until the heap is empty yields 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 9 in order: that is **heapsort**, n pops of O(log n) each, so O(n log n) even in the worst case, though not stable. The in-place version uses a max-heap and swaps each popped maximum into the slot that frees up at the end of the same array, and building the starting heap bottom-up takes only O(n). Heaps run priority queues and schedulers, timers, top-k queries (keep a heap of size k), merges of k sorted files and Dijkstra's shortest paths.
